strings.full_text:
In standard play on the default Humanity Ascendant mode, skilled and experienced AI War 2 players have found beachheading - building turrets on enemy planets - to be far more effective than relying primarily on mobile fleets and ships.  Expert Mode aims to achieve a more balanced approach in which beachheading can still be used but is not as overpowered as a strategy.

As you've probably noticed, you are restricted to a single battleship selection instead of the default two.  Additionally, hacking TSS for additional turrets will only grant them to the battlestation if you use the 3X option for just the battlestation.  When using the 1X option, those turrets will only be granted to your command stations, and the battlestation's complement will remain unchanged.

Beachheading is now more expensive; turrets on planets that are not player-owned costs 150% more to build, and have reduced range as well to limit the effectiveness of a variety of cheese tactics. The range reductions are as follows; infinite-range turrets reduced to 15k; turrets with over 11k range have a 30% reduction; those from 6k-11k are reduced 15%; below 6k are not reduced at all.
Note that losing a command station during a battle can be a major blow, since it could reduce the range of your turrets.

Finally, the amount of time that AI opponents must wait to utilize their full reinforcement cap has been reduced significantly, to counteract 'speed assassinations' in which the player could knock out a high-level AI before they had enough resources to truly fight back effectively.

This approach was arrived at in no small part due to the much-appreciated brainstorming and expertise of balance guru CRCGamer, and is a compromise solution that was the result of much debate and discussion.  Feedback is appreciated as always and tweaks are possible.  The goal is to continue allowing as many playstyles are possible, while not leaving a clear and major imbalanced strategy open to easy exploitation.

副手的玩法与死灵法师帝国相似，但有以下区别。首先，它必须与一个帝国阵营（人类帝国、方舟帝国、死灵法师帝国等）在同一星球上起始。其次，它本身不会失败；副手与它的帝国盟友同胜同负。

副手有一个实验性的自动防御模式（可通过死灵法师星系设置启用），能让其舰船自动协助盟友。

死灵法师仅适用于默认的“人类崛起”战役类型；“挑战者”及更高难度官方并不支持。

strings.full_text:
If you have units really far away from any planet you control, 5 hops minimum, there's a chance the AI Reserves will warp in to their location.

This is essentially a large AI force that aims to stop whatever sneaky shenanigans you're up to, being that far away from your territory. It gets larger as you move beyond that 5 hop minimum.

If you want to do such 'deepstrike' operations without them interrupting, you'll have to capture the occasional planet farther out, which extends the safe area.

The reserves spawn a seemingly endless flood of ships in greater and greater numbers the longer you deepstrike. Once you retreat though, they will all pull back to their wormholes and vanish.

You can use the galaxy map search bar (at the bottom center) to show which planets would trigger a deepstrike.

A subset of dedicated players enjoy this difficulty level, but it is not fun for most.  Beating the SuperCat even once is considered a crowning achievement, and usually involves a player discovering an unbalanced tactic.

This back-and-forth arms race between the players and the developers has led to some of the most interesting innovations for all levels of AI for the game (and its predecessor), and it is also a very specific style of brutal gauntlet that certain dedicated individuals enjoy throwing themselves into.

strings.full_text:
There are a few hacks that are planet-targeting, and which usually don't require any local hackers on your part.  You can just select an unexplored planet on the galaxy map, and then deploy spy nanites from the hacking sidebar tab, for instance.

Most hacks are ship/structure-targeting, however: there's some enemy unit that you can disrupt, capture for yourself, weaken, extract a benefit from... the list goes on.  For these you need to bring a hacker -- aka any Flagship of any of your mobile fleets -- and usually you need to keep the hacker in place for a short while.  The harder the hack, the longer you have to stick around.

Another common type of hack is against your own ships, and these tend to happen instantly.  This lets you deploy some of our limited cache of general-purpose nanobots for either reconfiguring or upgrading ships that tend to be the centerpieces of fleets.  Check in the fleet management pop-out for a given fleet by C-clicking it on your interface, or by opening it from the fleet management sidebar tab.

Fourth, we can spend some hacking points to retrieve spent science points ('science points' being another term of art that is explained in detail on the science point retrieval part of your HUD if you are interested) so that you can reallocate them.
       
Lastly, there are a very few hacks that you can run for a while and then cancel when you're ready to stop.  The SuperTerminal is the main example of this: you gain more and more benefit the longer you hack it, but more and more enemy forces rain down on you.  So you hack for as long as you think you can manage it, then cancel the hack and deal with the enemy that is now VERY aware of you.

指挥官，人工智能霸主已经变成了银河控制舰！它似乎暂时改变了相位，所以我们的武器无法击中它，它正在向我们的家园指挥站前进！在它重新进入与我们舰船的相位之前，我们将无法击中它。

我们认为相位变化只有在它在堡垒世界上时才是可持续的。这艘新的银河控制舰武装非常强大；我们可能需要一些新的策略来对付它。它似乎特别擅长摧毁攻击机。

Some planets can be fairly scary, their strength value far beyond everything you have combined. But! Most of that won't immediately attack you if you go in, and with a bit of thought, you can still win.
		
Instead, a good part of that is in stationary defenses such as Guard Posts and Turrets, then another large chunk are in guards stored inside those Posts.

If you're careful, you can move from area to area and clear them out, avoiding being in the range of any Guard Posts and Turrets, and not waking up the stored guards until ready. Even the Guardians, which like to patrol, you can intercept and fight on your own terms individually.

Lastly, take a look at the planet you're thinking of attacking. You might notice things such as the Guardians all have similar weaknesses or strengths, or every guard unit is something really fast, or is cloaked, etc. This can help you plan what to bring, and what to leave home.

strings.full_text:
指挥官，{PlanetName}上的联盟部队已经成功摧毁了一个黑暗尖塔族先锋。我们的扫描仪检测到一些废弃结构被炸到邻近星系，但它们看起来正在迅速衰变。

更有趣的是，每个戴森球似乎都在准备收集舰船出去为自己收集这些残骸。这些收集者似乎被各自球体的能量赋能，使它们对普通武器火力免疫。

我们的一些科学家认为，如果我们能将一个黑暗尖塔族残骸的力量与他们基于整个戴森球的设计结合起来，他们将能够为这些结构充能，使其能够向收集者开火。同样有用的是，他们相信这些设计以后可以重新用于保卫我们自己的星球。

虽然我们不认为自己能够超出这个范围实际利用这些残骸，但协助我们希望变得更强的任何球体将对我们有利。如果我们有任何这样做的愿望，我们的科学家建议你尽快派遣一艘战斗站到其中一个残骸星球。

There are multiple reasons for this. One is that we didn't want to reinvent the wheel and make a major change in how players acquire ships and turrets. This would have been an even greater shock to the system and required a much larger amount of work to reinvent items like capturable fleets, ARS and TSS that are hackable, and so on. The goal was to change as little as necessary from the way AI War 2 usually works.

Another reason is that the balance of power in Humanity Ascendant is significantly tilted in favor the player compared to earlier versions of AI War 2 or AI War 1 (Classic). Fuel seeks to restore that balance, and the only way to do that is to put in place measures that are effectively player nerfs in comparison to Humanity Ascendant.

It is often suggested to boost the AI instead of nerfing the player, but there's a practical limit on how much that can be done and still allow the game to run reasonably on PCs that most players use. It also would have skewed the power of the AI compared to the other factions, resulting in a wide range of knock-on affects. Some AI boosting is present for campaign types from Challenger on up in other features such as Dire CPAs, hacking exostrikes, increased Exo War unit budget, etc. 

Having said that, a major goal was to make the game more strategically interesting, not just more difficult. Player power is the element that was out of balance compared to the goals for Logistician and Deathwish campaigns, so that's where the effort primarily went on Fuel and other features of the new campaign types.

-Strategic Sage

指挥官，我们在银河系中发现了另一个奈因祖尔亚派系，玛瑙守护者。

珍珠守护者找不到词语来描述玛瑙带来的恐怖。虽然他们至少能够解释钻石对控制的渴望作为一种和平的方式，但玛瑙没有这样的迹象。他们没有长期目标，除了摧毁任何不屈服于他们的人，并且会乐于加入任何推动这一议程的团体。他们真的不尊重任何东西，只尊重力量，并且已经加入了新命名的'黑暗联盟'来压制我们的银河系。

In the first game, you had per-planet caps of turrets and other defenses.  You got more by unlocking new ship lines.
      
In this sequel, you get relatively little for defending yourself at the start of the game.  You can use battlestations and citadels, but there are very few of them in the galaxy.

Instead, what you want to do is hack Turret Schematic Servers (TSS) and Other Defensive Schematic Servers (ODSS).  TSS hacks grant additional turret lines, while ODSS hacks give you non-turret defensive structures such as mines, tractor arrays and gravity generators.  Keep in mind that hacking these servers requires twice as many hacking points if you don't own the planets where they are located.

This is basically the same sort of per-planet cap system as before, but it's driven by hacking AI servers rather than spending science.  You also have the option of adding these defensive options to your battlestations and citadels.  Doing this grants you three times the number of turrets or other structures, but as a global cap instead of a per-planet one.

Even beyond this, however, the type of command station you use gives you a bonus to per-planet caps:  Logistical get the default amount, Military get 2x the default amount, and Economic get half the normal amount.
strings.display_name: Turret Schematic Servers (TSSs) Are Critical For Defending

strings.full_text:
The Planet Sidebar has a number of ways it can display its data, and finding a style you prefer can make your gameplay experience much more comfortable. You can modify the display format with the Options menu at the very bottom of the planet sidebar.

When you open the Planet Menu it can show either the ships as Text (with names and icons) or as just icons.   

You can also choose how the ships are sorted when being displayed. You can sort them by faction, where each faction is listed individually (you can also have the per-faction view broken out by Mobile vs Stationary). You can also have it group the factions by their relationship with you (are they your allies? Your enemies?).

Finally, you can choose to show some of your Fleet information here. There are two types of Fleets for this sidebar; local fleets and Watched fleets. Local fleets are fleets whose centerpieces are on the planet you are currently looking at. Watched Fleets always appear regardless of which planet you are on. Watching important fleets is a great way to keep track of remote battles. 

When a fleet is displayed it will show its hotkey on the left. In the center is the name of the fleet and the flagship's current health (if it has taken damage). On the top right are the current strength of the fleet and what % of that fleet is still alive. And in the bottom right are the strengths of enemy and friendly forces on the flagship's current planet (if there are any enemies).

Hovering over a fleet in the sidebar will give you additional, more detailed information.
